Realism. A dominant movement of the nineteenth century that rejected the idealism and emotional excess of Romanticism in favor of precise, detailed depictions of ordinary life and contemporary society.

Realism emerged in mid-nineteenth century France as a deliberate reaction against Romanticism's idealization of nature, emotion, and the exotic. Gustave Flaubert's Madame Bovary, published in eighteen fifty-seven, became the movement's defining work. The central tenet was fidelity to observable fact. Realist authors aimed to record life with scientific precision, avoiding sentimentality, melodrama, and authorial judgment. Dialogue and setting were rendered with meticulous detail.

Realist novels typically featured protagonists of ordinary or modest station—clerks, provincial merchants, governesses, peasants—rather than aristocrats or extraordinary figures. Their inner lives and moral struggles were treated with full seriousness. Among the major practitioners were Balzac, Flaubert, George Eliot, Leo Tolstoy, and Fyodor Dostoevsky. Each developed the novel's capacity to explore psychology, society, and ethical complexity.

The movement expanded the novel's scope to encompass social analysis. Novels became accounts of how class, economics, marriage law, education, and institutions shaped individual destiny. A related movement called Naturalism, which emerged in the late nineteenth century, pushed realism even further by treating human behavior as determined by heredity and environment, employing what amounted to a quasi-scientific method in fiction. By century's end, realism had become the dominant mode of serious fiction in Europe. Even writers who moved beyond it—the symbolists and modernists—remained indebted to realism's formal innovations.
